extracted.intended_audience: poets, playwrights, dramatists, and students/scholars of poetics and literary theory
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and evaluative principles for composing poetry and especially Greek tragedy: what poetry imitates, the parts of tragedy, and how to construct plots, characters, diction, and spectacle to produce tragic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry as imitation (mimesis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry (including Epic, Tragedy, Comedy, Dithyrambic) is a mode of imitation: it imitates by rhythm, language, and harmony, singly or combined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle locates the essence of poetry in imitation: different arts differ in the medium, the objects, and the manner of imitation. This principle grounds all subsequent evaluative criteria (what is imitated and how).

rubrics_metrics.name: Three distinguishing factors: medium, objects, manner
rubrics_metrics.description: The arts differ from one another in three respects—the medium, the objects, the manner or mode of imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Medium: rhythm, language, harmony; Objects: types of persons/actions (noble, base, true-to-life); Manner: narration vs presentation (characters acting before us). Use these to classify and judge a poem's form and methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objects of imitation: represent men 'better, worse, or as they are'
rubrics_metrics.description: Poets must decide whether to represent people as better than in real life, worse than in real life, or as they are; this choice divides genres (Tragedy represents men better, Comedy worse).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Homer makes men better; Cleophon as they are; parody-makers worse. This affects tone, moral appeal, and suitability for tragic or comic treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manner of imitation: narration versus dramatic presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: A poet may imitate by narration (taking another personality or speaking in his own person) or by presenting characters living and moving before the audience (dramatic action).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dramatic presentation (action) is central to drama and changes requirements for plot and spectacle; narration suits epic/historical forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy definition and proper aim
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is an imitation of an action that is serious, complete, and of a certain magnitude, in language embellished with rhythm, harmony, and song, not of narrative but of action, producing through pity and fear the proper purgation (catharsis) of these emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This single-sentence definition sets the goal for tragic composition: seriousness, completeness, appropriate magnitude, ornamentation, action over narrative, and emotional effect (pity and fear leading to catharsis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Six constituent parts of Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Every Tragedy must have six parts—Plot, Character, Diction, Thought, Spectacle, Song—which together determine its quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle enumerates roles: Plot = arrangement of incidents (the soul); Character = qualities of agents; Diction = metrical arrangement of words; Thought = reasoning/proving/general truths; Song = musical elements/choric; Spectacle = visual elements (least artistic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of Plot (plot as soul of tragedy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot is the first principle and, as it were, the soul of a tragedy: the imitation of action, the arrangement of incidents, is most important—character is subsidiary to action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A play of finely written speeches can still fail if it lacks an artistically constructed plot. Emotional interest often depends on plot devices (peripeteia, recognition). Novices master diction before plot; experts must prioritize plot construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity and completeness (beginning, middle, end)
rubrics_metrics.description: A whole plot must have a beginning (nothing precedes it by necessity), a middle, and an end (nothing follows it); the parts must be organically connected so that removing any part disjoints the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unity of action—not unity of hero—is the requirement. Avoid including unrelated episodes even if they all happen to the same character (e.g., avoid compiling disconnected adventures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper magnitude / appropriate length
rubrics_metrics.description: The plot must be of a magnitude that can be grasped in a single view or memory: not so short as to be confused, nor so long that the unity of the whole is lost; roughly, tragedy should aim for a length that permits a sequence of events allowing a change of fortune.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tragedy traditionally aims to confine itself to about a single revolution of the sun; epic has no strict limits. Magnitude contributes to beauty by allowing order and unity to be perceived.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability and necessity in sequence of events
rubrics_metrics.description: Poets should represent what may happen according to the law of probability or necessity rather than merely what has happened; events in the plot should follow as necessary or probable results of preceding actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A poet constructs the universal (what a person of a certain type would do) not merely the particular. Avoid sequences that are arbitrary or merely coincidental; surprise is best when it appears as designed rather than accidental.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of epeisodic plots
rubrics_metrics.description: Epeisodic plots—where episodes succeed without probable or necessary sequence—are the worst kind; they lack organic unity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad poets compose such episodes for show or players; good poets avoid stretching plots beyond their capacity and breaking natural continuity for spectacle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple versus Complex plots
rubrics_metrics.description: Plots are Simple when change of fortune occurs without Reversal or Recognition. Complex plots involve Reversal (peripeteia), Recognition (anagnorisis), or both, arising from the internal structure so that events are the necessary or probable result of prior action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A perfect tragedy should be complex: Reversal and Recognition heighten pity and fear when organically produced by the plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peripeteia (Reversal of the Situation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Reversal is a change by which the action veers round to its opposite, subject to rules of probability or necessity (e.g., messenger meant to help Oedipus instead causes his ruin).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reversals should follow from the plot's internal logic, not be arbitrary. They are a primary source of tragic wonder and emotional effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition (Anagnorisis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition is a change from ignorance to knowledge producing love or hate; the best form coincides with Reversal, producing maximum pity/fear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognitions may involve persons or even inanimate signs; they must be connected intimately to the plot and contribute to the change of fortune.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene of suffering
rubrics_metrics.description: The Scene of Suffering is a destructive or painful action (death on stage, bodily agony, wounds) and is a part of plot structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such scenes can be effective, but the highest tragic effect arises when suffering and its causes are embedded in the plot's internal necessity rather than staged for mere spectacle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragic emotional aim: arouse pity and fear and effect purgation
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy should imitate actions that inspire pity and fear, and through these emotions effect the proper purgation (catharsis) of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plots that provoke pity and fear are those where misfortune befalls a person like ourselves and results from error rather than vice. Producing these emotions through inner plot structure is superior to relying on spectacle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate tragic subject / protagonist (neither perfect good nor villain)
rubrics_metrics.description: The protagonist should not be eminently good or wholly wicked; the misfortune should arise not from vice but from some error or frailty (hamartia) in a person of high repute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The tragic hero's fall by error arouses pity (unmerited misfortune) and fear (it could happen to us). Avoid portraying virtuous men brought to ruin by fate (shocking but not tragic) or villains punished (satisfying but not tragic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Single issue ending and preferable direction of change
rubrics_metrics.description: A well constructed plot should be single in issue rather than double; the change of fortune should be from good to bad rather than the reverse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Double-thread plots that give opposite catastrophes for good and bad are inferior and cater to weakness of spectators; they produce less authentic tragic pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character criteria: goodness, propriety, truth to life, consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Character should (1) be good (manifest moral purpose), (2) show propriety (appropriate traits for the class), (3) be true to life (realistic), and (4) be consistent—even if consistently inconsistent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speech and action express character. Avoid motiveless degradation or traits inappropriate to the character's social type (e.g., manly valor in a woman). Consistency can allow for flawed figures but must be coherent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought (dianoia) as proof and expression of what is possible and pertinent
rubrics_metrics.description: Thought is the faculty of saying what is possible and pertinent in given circumstances—where something is proved, or a general truth enunciated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thought functions similarly to rhetoric/oratory in showing reasons; speeches that do not reveal choice or avoidance are not expressive of character. Thought contributes to the intellectual force of the play.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction (lexis): expression of meaning in words and metrical arrangement
rubrics_metrics.description: Diction is the expression of the meaning in words, essentially the metrical arrangement of words in verse or prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good diction renders meaning clearly and artistically; it is subordinate to plot and thought but necessary for poetic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Song (melos) as chief embellishment
rubrics_metrics.description: Song holds the chief place among the embellishments associated with language; it is an important component in parts rendered with the aid of song.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Song contributes strongly to the emotional and formal coloring of tragedy (choral odes etc.), but remains an embellishment supporting the action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spectacle: least artistic but emotionally attractive
rubrics_metrics.description: Spectacle (the visual elements) has emotional attraction but is the least artistic part of tragedy and is least connected with the poet's art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spectacular effects rely more on stagecraft than on poetry: tragic power should be felt even without representation. Relying on spectacle to produce horror/monstrosity is a less artistic method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative/structural parts of tragedy (prologue, episode, exode, parode, stasimon, commos)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is divided into quantitative parts: Prologue (before Parode), Episode (between choric songs), Exode (no choric song after it), Parode (first chorus utterance), Stasimon (choric ode without certain metres), Commos (joint lamentation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are formal divisions every poet should understand when structuring a play; some plays also include actor songs from the stage. Use them to allocate where diction, song, and choral elements appear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation of Epic and Tragedy (shared elements and differences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic poetry and Tragedy share many elements (both imitate serious actions and noble characters) but differ in metre (epic admits one metre) and form (epic is narrative and not confined by time to a single day), while Tragedy presents action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knowing the overlap helps transfer principles across genres: those who know good Tragedy understand Epic. However, not all tragic elements are present in epic and the demands on unity differ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origins and psychological basis of poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry stems from natural instincts: the instinct to imitate and the instinct for rhythm and harmony; humans take pleasure in imitation and learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This anthropological claim grounds why imitation and rhythm are pleasurable and should be harnessed by the poet when crafting works that teach and move the audience.
